This remarkable place is known for its clear turquoise waters, lush tropical vegetation, and unusual shoreline covered with millions of tiny white and pinkish shells instead of ordinary sand.

The beach's name reflects its defining feature: the word conchal is associated with seashells, which have shaped the coast's distinctive appearance over many years. The contrast between the pale shoreline, azure ocean, and green hills creates a picture-postcard scene.

Playa Conchal is ideal for swimming, snorkeling, and exploring the underwater world of the Pacific Ocean. In the calm coastal waters, you can watch colorful tropical fish, while those who enjoy walking will appreciate the scenic surroundings and secluded stretches of coast.

The beach is particularly charming at sunset, when sunlight turns the ocean golden and pink. It is easy to forget everyday concerns here while enjoying the sound of the surf, the warm sea breeze, and the tranquility of a tropical retreat.

Playa Conchal is an ideal destination for anyone dreaming of discovering Costa Rica's natural beauty, spending time by the ocean, and experiencing the harmony of a tropical paradise.

After a long trek through the valley, the tents of Plaza de Mulas look like a small town in the Andes. Groups from around the world meet on the rocky plateau, gear is hung out to dry, and upcoming ascents are discussed. Hot food and the chance to take off your boots feel especially welcome here. Vast slopes and snow-covered high ridges surround the camp.

Plaza de Mulas sits at approximately 4,300 m and serves as the base camp for the normal route up Aconcagua. Hikers reach it through the Horcones Valley and Confluencia. The camp can also be a destination for a separate multi-day trek: travelers experience an expedition setting even if they leave the summit climb to mountaineers.

On Ada Tours itineraries, days here are devoted to rest and preparation for higher camps. From Plaza de Mulas, the group hikes to Bonete Peak and makes acclimatization treks. Mules carry part of the load on the approach; camp setup, meals, and the work of the support team depend on the tour chosen. Overnight stays at this altitude require gradual ascent and attention to how you feel.

The square's main feature, the Monument to the Two Congresses, commemorates the Assembly of 1813 and the Congress of Tucumán in 1816. Its stone pedestal, sculptures, and fountain form a monumental composition best appreciated from several angles.

The square was designed by Carlos Thays, and its inauguration was timed to coincide with the centenary of the May Revolution. The green space continues into neighboring squares. Fountains, lawns, and paths provide a welcome pause amid busy streets.

On a sightseeing tour, this is a convenient place to discuss the country's political system and the capital's architecture. Exploring the square means seeing its outdoor public spaces; a visit to the interior of the parliament building must be arranged separately.
